unit.title: Perpetual review
unit.summary: Spaced retrieval of mastered concepts across the whole course.

lessons.title: Daily Bite
lessons.objective: Retrieve five due concepts in about two minutes.

payload.prompt: How many points does a Grand Prix win score?

options.text: 25 points
options.explanation: Right. A win is 25, then 18 for second and 15 for third.

options.text: 20 points
options.explanation: Not any more. The scale has been 25 for a win since 2010.

options.text: 18 points plus one for fastest lap
options.explanation: Eighteen is second place, and the fastest-lap point was dropped from 2025.

options.text: 15 points
options.explanation: Fifteen is third place. The winner gets 25.

explanation.correct: A win is worth 25 points, and the top ten score 25-18-15-12-10-8-6-4-2-1.
explanation.incorrect: A win scores 25. Second scores 18, third 15, and there is no extra point for fastest lap.
explanation.sayThisLine: A win is twenty-five points.

payload.prompt: Why does an undercut gain time on a rival?

options.text: The car behind stops first, gets fresh tyres, and is faster on the next lap.
options.explanation: Right. Fresh rubber beats old tyres for pace.

options.text: The pit lane is shorter if you pit early.
options.explanation: No, the pit lane does not change length mid-race.

options.text: Fresh tyres are automatically faster by a fixed amount.
options.explanation: Not automatic. Pace gain depends on how old the old tyres are.

options.text: It saves fuel, which makes the car lighter.
options.explanation: F1 has not had refuelling since 2010.

explanation.correct: Right. The first to pit gets fresh grip while rivals are on old tyres.
explanation.incorrect: An undercut works because fresh tyres are faster than worn tyres.
explanation.sayThisLine: Pit first, get fresh tyres, jump ahead when they stop.

payload.prompt: How does downforce help a race car in a corner?

options.text: It pushes the car into the track, increasing grip.
options.explanation: Right. Downforce = more grip = faster cornering.

options.text: It keeps the car from flipping over.
options.explanation: Downforce does add stability, but the main benefit is grip for speed.

options.text: It pushes the driver back in the seat for comfort.
options.explanation: Downforce affects the car's grip, not the driver's comfort.

options.text: It reduces drag so the car accelerates faster.
options.explanation: No, downforce brings drag as a side effect. Drag slows.

explanation.correct: Right. Downforce = grip = ability to go fast through corners.
explanation.incorrect: Downforce is aerodynamic force that pushes the car into the track.
explanation.sayThisLine: More downforce means the car can corner faster.

payload.prompt: Complete the safety car sentence.
payload.template: When a safety car is deployed, it {{result}} the field by slowing everyone to the same pace.

explanation.correct: Right. The safety car bunches the pack, erasing the gaps built up in the race.
explanation.incorrect: A safety car bunches the field, closing up all the gaps between cars.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: The wings open on the straights and close for the corners. It is like a two-speed wing.

payload.question: What is she describing?

options.text: Active aero: Straight Mode for low drag and Corner Mode for grip.
options.explanation: Yes. The wings move to trade drag against downforce as the lap changes.

options.text: A pit-stop routine for changing the wings.
options.explanation: The wings move while the car is on track, not in the pits.

options.text: A mechanical failure that makes the wings flap.
options.explanation: It is a designed feature of the 2026 cars.

options.text: A penalty for running the wing too low.
options.explanation: It is not a penalty. It is how the cars work.

payload.translation: The 2026 cars have moving wings. On straights they go to low drag, and for braking and corners they return to the high-downforce setting.

followUps.line: Is the switch manual or automatic?
followUps.why: A genuine question about how active aero is controlled.

followUps.line: Was that what DRS did?
followUps.why: DRS only opened one flap for a chasing car. Active aero is for everyone.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If you are not sure about the details, ask how the switching works.

lessons.title: Weekend recap review
lessons.objective: Refresh the concepts that appeared in the latest race.

payload.prompt: Why is a pit stop under a safety car called 'cheap'?

options.text: Because the pit crew is paid less under a safety car.
options.explanation: No, the crew is the same. The pit lane cost is lower.

options.text: Because the cost in time is much smaller than a normal stop.
options.explanation: Right. The field is slow, so stopping costs less lap time.

options.text: Because no tyres are changed during a safety car.
options.explanation: No, teams do change tyres; the pit lane is just slower.

options.text: Because the team does not have to pay for fuel.
options.explanation: F1 has not had refuelling since 2010. Wrong era.

explanation.correct: Right. Under a safety car, the whole field is slowed, so pit-lane time loss is small.
explanation.incorrect: A cheap stop under a safety car costs less time because the field is slow.
explanation.sayThisLine: Under the safety car, the pit stop is cheap.

payload.prompt: What does tyre degradation mean in a Grand Prix?

options.text: The tyre loses grip and lap time as the stint goes on.
options.explanation: Right. Tyre wear is the main variable in race strategy.

options.text: The tyre completely fails and forces a DNF.
options.explanation: Degradation is slow loss of grip, not sudden failure.

options.text: The tyre pressure drops because of the heat.
options.explanation: Pressure is monitored and managed; deg is the grip loss.

options.text: The tyre looks discoloured after the race.
options.explanation: Colour change does not define degradation. It is lap-time loss.

explanation.correct: Right. Tyres get slower lap by lap. Managing this is strategy.
explanation.incorrect: Degradation is the gradual loss of grip and speed as tyres age.
explanation.sayThisLine: His fronts are degrading; pace has dropped.

payload.prompt: What does a five-second time penalty mean in a race?

options.text: Five seconds is added to the driver's race time, often served at a pit stop.
options.explanation: Right. The driver's finishing order is worked out after the time is added.

options.text: The driver starts five places lower at the next race.
options.explanation: That is a grid penalty, which is a different thing.

options.text: The whole race is paused for five seconds.
options.explanation: Only the penalised driver is affected.

options.text: The driver loses five championship points.
options.explanation: Time penalties change the order, not the points directly.

explanation.correct: Five seconds added to the finishing time can drop a driver several places if the gaps behind are small.
explanation.incorrect: A time penalty adds seconds to a driver's race time. The classification is worked out with the extra time included.
explanation.sayThisLine: Five seconds could cost him two places.

payload.prompt: Complete the tyre sentence.
payload.template: If tyres {{condition}} too quickly, the team must pit earlier than planned.

explanation.correct: Right. Fast degradation forces an early stop to avoid the tyre cliff.
explanation.incorrect: If tyres degrade too fast, the team has to pit earlier than planned.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: Ten seconds for that? He only barely touched him. That is so harsh.

payload.question: What is she talking about?

options.text: She thinks a ten-second penalty is too steep for light contact.
options.explanation: Yes. She believes the penalty does not fit the incident.

options.text: The stewards gave the wrong driver a penalty.
options.explanation: She is not questioning who got penalised, but the amount.

options.text: She wants a grid penalty instead of a time penalty.
options.explanation: Not mentioned. She is about the size of the penalty.

options.text: The penalty was applied at the wrong time.
options.explanation: Timing is not her concern; it is the severity.

payload.translation: She thinks the stewards gave a too-harsh time penalty for a minor collision.

followUps.line: What penalty would you have given for that kind of contact?
followUps.why: Asks her opinion rather than correcting; stewards' calls are always debated.

followUps.line: Did it change the race result for him?
followUps.why: Focuses on the consequence rather than the rule.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Penalty consistency is the top fan debate; there is no single 'right' call.

lessons.title: Term retrieval mix
lessons.objective: Match and complete terms from every layer, weakest first.

payload.prompt: Match team and engine concepts.

pairs.definition: A team that builds and races its own car.
The turbocharged engine plus electrical systems driving the car.
Works team makes its engine; customer team buys power from another.

distractorDefinitions: The fuel that powers F1 cars.

explanation.summary: Constructor builds the car; power unit is the engine. Works = own engine.
explanation.sayThisLine: Ferrari is a constructor with its own power unit.

payload.prompt: Match strategy and racing terms.

pairs.definition: The range of laps in which a pit stop makes strategic sense.
Drafting behind a car ahead to cut drag and gain speed.
The turbulent wake that steals grip from the following car.

explanation.summary: Pit window is when to stop, the slipstream is the tow gain, and dirty air is the price of following closely.
explanation.sayThisLine: The pit window is closing, and the slipstream is hard to find in dirty air.

payload.prompt: Which championship is for teams?
payload.template: The {{award}} Championship is won by the team that scores the most points across both drivers.

explanation.correct: Right. The Constructors' Championship adds both drivers' points. The Drivers' Championship is individual.
explanation.incorrect: It is the Constructors' Championship for teams. The Drivers' Championship is for individuals.

payload.prompt: Complete the tow sentence.
payload.template: The {{effect}} behind a car ahead lets the following driver cut drag on the straight.

explanation.correct: Right. The slipstream, or tow, cuts drag and lets the car behind gain speed down the straight.
explanation.incorrect: The slipstream, also called the tow, is what reduces drag for the car behind.

payload.prompt: What does it mean if a pit window is 'open'?

options.text: Now is a good time to pit based on tyre life and track position.
options.explanation: Right. The window is the laps where a stop makes tactical sense.

options.text: The pit lane has no traffic.
options.explanation: No, traffic can vary. The window is about timing in the race.

options.text: The team has no pit crew available.
options.explanation: Wrong. An open window means conditions are right to pit.

options.text: A safety car has just deployed.
options.explanation: Safety cars change pit timing but do not define the window.

explanation.correct: Right. When the pit window is open, stopping gains you places or position.
explanation.incorrect: A pit window is the range of laps where a pit stop makes strategic sense.
explanation.sayThisLine: The pit window is open; time to pit.

payload.prompt: When is the slipstream most useful in a race?

options.text: On long straights where the tow lets you catch up and overtake.
options.explanation: Right. The slipstream gives extra speed on the straight.

options.text: In tight corners where drafting tightens your line.
options.explanation: No, the tow is a straight-line effect. Corners lose the benefit.

options.text: During a pit stop when the car is slow.
options.explanation: The pit stop is not where you use aerodynamic effects.

options.text: Under a safety car when the field is bunched.
options.explanation: Bunching does not create more slipstream benefit than a normal race.

explanation.correct: Right. The tow on a straight is the classic overtaking setup.
explanation.incorrect: The slipstream works on straights where drag is the limiting factor.
explanation.sayThisLine: He got a tow down the back straight and pulled off an overtake.

lessons.title: Say-this refresher
lessons.objective: Decode fan lines you have already met, in new wording.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: He is within a second at the detection point. Overtake Mode is on!

payload.question: What is she talking about?

options.text: He is close enough to get an electrical boost to attack the car ahead.
options.explanation: Yes. Within one second at the detection point makes him eligible for Overtake Mode.

options.text: He is close enough to use the DRS flap.
options.explanation: DRS ended in 2025. Overtake Mode replaced it in 2026.

options.text: He is about to pit under a safety car.
options.explanation: She is talking about a passing attempt, not a pit stop.

options.text: He has one lap left before he gets penalty points.
options.explanation: It has nothing to do with penalties.

payload.translation: He is close enough to the car ahead at the detection point to get extra electrical power, which should help him attack on the straight.

followUps.line: Does Overtake Mode guarantee a pass?
followUps.why: It does not. Dirty air and timing matter as well.

followUps.line: How is that different from DRS?
followUps.why: A natural follow-up that shows you know what changed.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Overtake Mode is a boost, not a guarantee. Ask if he made the pass.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: His best lap was deleted. Four wheels over the line at turn three on his flying lap.

payload.question: What is she talking about?

options.text: His qualifying or practice lap was cancelled for exceeding track limits.
options.explanation: Yes. Going outside the white lines voids the lap time.

options.text: He crashed and his car had to be repaired.
options.explanation: Deleted laps are about rules, not crashes.

options.text: A technical issue made the data invalid.
options.explanation: Track limits are rule-based, not technical failures.

options.text: The stewards gave him a time penalty instead.
options.explanation: Lap deletion is the track-limits consequence; no extra penalty needed.

payload.translation: His fastest qualifying or practice lap was cancelled because he drove outside the white line boundaries of the track.

followUps.line: Is he allowed to use the kerbs?
followUps.why: Asks about the boundary definition; kerbs are usually OK.

followUps.line: Can he appeal a deleted lap?
followUps.why: Shows interest in the consequence rather than judgment.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Track limits are marked by white lines; kerbs are usually fair game.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: That stint was 28 laps on softs. No way the tyres last that long. He will pit soon.

payload.question: What is she talking about?

options.text: She thinks the driver will need to pit within the next few laps because soft tyres cannot last 28 laps.
options.explanation: Yes. She is predicting tyre degradation will force a stop.

options.text: The pit stop is mandatory every 28 laps.
options.explanation: There is no fixed lap rule for stops; it is strategy and tyre life.

options.text: Soft tyres are not allowed in races.
options.explanation: Softs are allowed and often used; they just wear faster.

options.text: The team will add fuel during the stop.
options.explanation: F1 has not refuelled since 2010.

payload.translation: She is saying the driver has been on soft tyres for 28 laps, which is unsustainable due to tyre wear, so he will need to pit soon for fresh tyres.

followUps.line: Why would they choose soft tyres if they degrade so fast?
followUps.why: Asks about the trade-off: softs are quick but short-lived.

followUps.line: Could he be saving them for a later push?
followUps.why: Shows strategic thinking about tyre pacing.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Soft tyres are fast but have short life; managing this trade-off is the race.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: He hit the boost button too early on the straight and wasted it before the braking zone where he could have passed.

payload.question: What is she talking about?

options.text: He used his limited boost at the wrong moment for a passing attempt.
options.explanation: Yes. Boost is a driver button that is limited in how often it can be used, so timing matters.

options.text: He pitted at the wrong time.
options.explanation: She is talking about the boost button, not a pit stop.

options.text: He left his wings open in the braking zone.
options.explanation: Boost is electrical deployment, not a wing mode.

options.text: He got a penalty for pressing the button.
options.explanation: Using boost is allowed. Bad timing is just poor strategy.

payload.translation: He pushed the boost button too soon, so the extra electrical power was spent before the place where it would have helped him pass.

followUps.line: Is boost unlimited?
followUps.why: It is limited in how much and how often a driver can use it, so each use counts.

followUps.line: Could the engineer have told him when?
followUps.why: Teams give advice over the radio, so it is a fair question about teamwork.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Boost timing is a skill. If you are unsure, ask what he should have waited for.

payload.title: Stint strategy chat
payload.setting: Talking about the race strategy after qualifying.

exchanges.theirMessage: I think they will go for a long first stint on the hards. Three-stop race, maybe.

replies.text: Three stops is aggressive. Do you think the hard tyres can make it 25 laps?
replies.theirResponse: If they nurse them, yeah. They are trying to undercut the guys on softs.
replies.coachNote: You asked a specific question about tyre life, showing you understand stint length.

replies.theirResponse: It really is. Lots to think about.
replies.coachNote: Not wrong, but generic. Ask about their reasoning.

replies.text: Three stops seems like a waste. They should just go for the one-stop like everyone else.
replies.theirResponse: Not everyone goes one-stop. Track temps, degradation, the field changes the call.
replies.coachNote: Oversimplifying strategy. Each race has different rules and conditions.

payload.closingNote: A stint is a stretch of laps on one set of tyres; strategy is about when to stop.

lessons.title: Flags and officials refresh
lessons.objective: Retrieve the flags, neutralisations and who makes the calls.

payload.prompt: A lapped car sees a blue flag. What must it do?

scene.alt: Text only: a slower, lapped car is shown a blue flag as the race leader approaches.

explanation.correct: A blue flag means a faster car is about to lap you. The driver has to let it through quickly, or risk a penalty.
explanation.incorrect: Blue flags are an instruction to let faster, lapping cars past. Ignoring them can bring a penalty.
explanation.sayThisLine: He got the blue flag, so he has to get out of the way.

payload.prompt: Match each flag to its message.

pairs.definition: Danger ahead: slow down and no overtaking in that zone.
The session is stopped, and cars return to the pit lane.
A driver is disqualified and must come into the pits.
A faster car is behind: let it through.

distractorDefinitions: The pit crew is ready to start the stop.
The driver has set the fastest lap.

explanation.summary: Yellow warns, red stops, black disqualifies and blue asks you to move over. Four colours, four very different messages.
explanation.sayThisLine: Yellow means careful, red means stop.

payload.prompt: Who does what in race control?
payload.template: The {{boss}} runs the race and calls the safety car, while the {{panel}} decides penalties.

explanation.correct: The race director manages the session and its neutralisations. The stewards investigate incidents and decide penalties.
explanation.incorrect: The race director runs the race and deploys safety cars. The stewards are the panel that judges incidents and hands out penalties.
explanation.sayThisLine: The stewards are looking at it.

payload.prompt: What makes a virtual safety car different from a real one?

options.text: Drivers slow to a set pace where they are, and no pace car bunches the field.
options.explanation: Right. The gaps stay roughly the same, unlike under the real safety car.

options.text: A second, smaller safety car leads the midfield.
options.explanation: There is no second car. The virtual one is a speed rule, not a vehicle.

options.text: Everyone must pit at once.
options.explanation: Pitting is optional, and the stop is cheaper, but nobody has to come in.

options.text: It is used only at the start of a race.
options.explanation: It is used when a problem needs a short neutralisation, at any time.

explanation.correct: Under a virtual safety car everyone slows to a set pace and keeps their gaps. Under the real safety car, the field bunches behind it.
explanation.incorrect: A virtual safety car is a mandatory slow pace on track, not a pace car, so the gaps stay the same.
explanation.sayThisLine: The VSC freezes the gaps; the real safety car erases them.

payload.prompt: Complete the ban rule.
payload.template: Reaching {{points}} penalty points within {{months}} months means a {{ban}}.

explanation.correct: Twelve penalty points within twelve months bring a one-race ban, and each point drops off after a year.
explanation.incorrect: The threshold is twelve points in twelve months, which brings a one-race ban.
explanation.sayThisLine: One more point and he is banned.

lessons.title: Car and corner refresh
lessons.objective: Retrieve how a car corners and what keeps the driver safe.

payload.prompt: The front will not turn in and the car runs wide. What is it called?

options.text: Understeer
options.explanation: Right. The front tyres run out of grip and the car pushes wide.

options.text: Oversteer
options.explanation: Oversteer is when the rear steps out and the car spins tighter.

options.text: Porpoising
options.explanation: Porpoising is the car bouncing on a straight, not running wide in a corner.

options.text: Graining
options.explanation: Graining is tyre damage, not a handling description.

explanation.correct: Understeer is when the front does not bite, so the car runs wide. Oversteer is the rear stepping out.
explanation.incorrect: When the front refuses to turn, that is understeer. Oversteer is the opposite, with the rear sliding.
explanation.sayThisLine: He had understeer and ran wide.

payload.prompt: Does more downforce always make a car quicker round a lap?

scene.alt: Text only: more downforce gives more grip but also more drag.

explanation.correct: More downforce means more grip, but also more drag, so the car is slower on the straights. Teams balance the two for each track.
explanation.incorrect: Downforce helps in the corners but adds drag, which slows the car on straights. That trade-off decides the set-up.
explanation.sayThisLine: More wing is faster in the corners and slower on the straights.

payload.prompt: Match the term to what it is.

pairs.definition: The carbon-fibre survival cell the driver sits in.
A titanium bar over the cockpit that protects the driver's head.
The painted edges of the corner that drivers can use, within limits.
The path round a corner that lets the car go fastest.

distractorDefinitions: The part of the pit lane where tyres are stored.

explanation.summary: The monocoque and halo keep the driver safe, while kerbs and the racing line decide how quick a corner can be.
explanation.sayThisLine: He took the kerb and stayed on the racing line.

payload.prompt: Put a corner in order.
payload.template: A driver {{first}} in the braking zone, turns in, clips the {{point}}, then gets back on the {{last}} on exit.

explanation.correct: Brake in a straight line, turn in, touch the apex on the inside, then return to the throttle as the car straightens.
explanation.incorrect: The order is brake, turn in, reach the apex on the inside, then back on the throttle.
explanation.sayThisLine: Brake, turn in, apex, throttle.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: He clipped the apex on every lap. Look at the tidy line he takes.

payload.question: What is she praising?

options.text: He touched the inside point of the corner each lap, which is the fastest, cleanest line.
options.explanation: Yes. The apex is the point closest to the inside of the corner.

options.text: He drove along the outside edge of the track.
options.explanation: That is the opposite of the apex.

options.text: He used the pit lane on every lap.
options.explanation: The apex is a place on the corner, not the pit lane.

options.text: He always used the wings at the same time.
options.explanation: The apex is about the line through a corner, not the wings.

payload.translation: He hit the same inside point of the corner on every lap, which means he drove a consistent, efficient line.

followUps.line: Is that hard to do lap after lap?
followUps.why: A real question: consistency is a big part of being quick.

followUps.line: Does the apex change with the car?
followUps.why: A good way to ask about how set-up affects the line.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You do not need to name the corner. Asking whether the line is hard to repeat is enough.

lessons.title: Racecraft and strategy refresh
lessons.objective: Retrieve how passing and pit calls really work.

payload.prompt: What is a dive-bomb?

options.text: A very late, deep braking move to pass on the inside.
options.explanation: Right. It is bold and risky, and it does not always come off.

options.text: A pit stop made at the last possible second.
options.explanation: That is a late stop, not a dive-bomb.

options.text: A driver leaving the track to gain time.
options.explanation: That is a track-limits problem.

options.text: A safety car starting a race.
options.explanation: It is unrelated to safety cars.

explanation.correct: A dive-bomb is braking very late, deep into a corner, to pass on the inside before the rival can respond.
explanation.incorrect: A dive-bomb is a late, deep braking move into a corner to pass on the inside.
explanation.sayThisLine: He dive-bombed him at turn one.

payload.prompt: May a driver zigzag repeatedly to block a chasing car?

scene.alt: Text only: a leading driver weaves across the track to block a chaser.

choices.label: Yes, as much as he likes

explanation.correct: A driver may move once to defend, but repeated weaving to block is not allowed and can bring a penalty.
explanation.incorrect: Defending is allowed, but only one change of direction. Weaving to block a chaser is penalised.
explanation.sayThisLine: He moved once to defend, which is fine. Two moves is weaving.

payload.prompt: Match each strategy move to what it is.

pairs.definition: Pitting first so fresh tyres let you jump ahead.
Staying out longer in clear air, then stopping and coming out ahead.
Choosing a different tyre or stop plan from the car next to you.
Two teammates pitting on back-to-back laps, so the second car waits.

distractorDefinitions: A rule that decides who starts on pole.
A penalty for speeding in the pit lane.

explanation.summary: Undercut and overcut are about timing, offset is about a different plan, and double stack is a risk when both cars pit together.
explanation.sayThisLine: They split the strategies so one could overcut.

payload.prompt: Complete the dirty air sentence.
payload.template: Dirty air steals a following car's {{what}}, which is why staying close in {{where}} corners is so hard.

explanation.correct: The car ahead leaves turbulent air that cuts the follower's downforce. That hurts most in fast corners, where grip is essential.
explanation.incorrect: Dirty air reduces the downforce of the car behind, and fast corners depend most on downforce.
explanation.sayThisLine: He could not follow through the fast corners.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: They pitted him early just to cover the undercut.

payload.question: What did the team do?

options.text: Stopped him to stay ahead of a rival who had stopped, rather than waiting.
options.explanation: Yes. Covering means responding to a rival's stop before the undercut can work.

options.text: Hid his car from the cameras.
options.explanation: Covering is about position, not cameras.

options.text: Gave him a penalty.
options.explanation: A pit stop is not a penalty.

options.text: Started a virtual safety car.
options.explanation: Only race control can start that.

payload.translation: The team pitted him soon after a rival did, so the rival could not use fresh tyres to jump ahead.

followUps.line: Did it work?
followUps.why: A simple question that keeps the focus on the result.

followUps.line: What would have happened if he had stayed out?
followUps.why: It asks about the trade-off without pretending to know.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If the jargon loses you, ask which car pitted first.

lessons.title: Energy and rules refresh
lessons.objective: Retrieve the 2026 power unit, energy ideas and rules politics.

payload.prompt: Which part was removed from the power unit for 2026?

options.text: The MGU-H
options.explanation: Right. The heat-recovery unit was deleted to simplify the power unit.

options.text: The MGU-K
options.explanation: The MGU-K stays and is now more powerful.

options.text: The turbocharger
options.explanation: The turbo is still there. Only the heat-recovery unit went.

options.text: The battery
options.explanation: The energy store is still essential.

explanation.correct: The MGU-H, the unit that recovered energy from exhaust heat, was deleted for 2026. The MGU-K and the turbo remain.
explanation.incorrect: The MGU-H was the part that went. The MGU-K became bigger and does more of the work.
explanation.sayThisLine: The MGU-H is gone for 2026.

payload.prompt: Complete the fuel sentence.
payload.template: F1's 2026 fuel is {{share}} sustainable, made from non-food biomass, waste or captured {{what}}.

explanation.correct: From 2026 F1 uses fully sustainable fuel, made from non-food biomass, waste or captured carbon.
explanation.incorrect: The 2026 fuel is 100% advanced sustainable fuel, made from non-food sources, waste or captured carbon.
explanation.sayThisLine: The fuel is fully sustainable now.

payload.prompt: Does lift and coast make a car quicker that lap?

scene.alt: Text only: a driver lifts off early before a braking zone.

explanation.correct: Lift and coast costs a little time on that lap, in exchange for saving fuel, energy or brakes for later.
explanation.incorrect: Lifting early is slower on that lap. Teams accept it to save something for later in the race.
explanation.sayThisLine: He is lifting and coasting, so he is giving up a bit of time.

payload.prompt: Match each energy word to what it means.

pairs.definition: Refilling the battery, mainly under braking.
The car stops accelerating on a long straight because the battery is low.
A driver button for extra electrical power, used sparingly.
Lifting off early to save fuel, energy or brakes.

distractorDefinitions: A tyre compound made for wet races.
A penalty for using too much fuel.

explanation.summary: 2026 racing is energy management. Recharge puts energy in, boost and deployment spend it, and clipping shows when it ran out.
explanation.sayThisLine: He harvested in the braking zone and boosted on the straight.

payload.prompt: What does the cost cap do?

options.text: It limits how much a team can spend on running its car in a year, with some exceptions.
options.explanation: Right. It is a yearly budget limit, with carve-outs such as driver pay.

options.text: It caps the price of race tickets.
options.explanation: Ticket prices are not part of it.

options.text: It sets the maximum fuel each car can use.
options.explanation: Fuel use is a separate technical rule.

options.text: It limits how many races a team can enter.
options.explanation: Every team enters every race.

explanation.correct: The cost cap is a yearly limit on team spending, around 215 million dollars, with carve-outs. Breaches bring fines and sporting penalties.
explanation.incorrect: The cost cap is a budget limit on spending, not a limit on tickets, fuel or races.
explanation.sayThisLine: The cost cap stops money deciding everything.

payload.prompt: Complete the weight fact.
payload.template: The 2026 minimum weight is about {{kg}} kg, lighter than before.

explanation.correct: The 2026 cars are lighter, with a minimum weight of about 768 kg, around 30 kg less than before.
explanation.incorrect: The minimum weight fell to about 768 kg for 2026.
explanation.sayThisLine: The 2026 cars are smaller and lighter.

lessons.title: Paddock and history refresh
lessons.objective: Retrieve who does what in the paddock and the key history.

payload.prompt: Can a driver race in F1 without a super licence?

scene.alt: Text only: a young driver who has not earned the FIA licence.

explanation.correct: The FIA requires a super licence, which is earned through points in approved junior series such as F2 and F3.
explanation.incorrect: A super licence is mandatory, and it has to be earned with results in junior series.
explanation.sayThisLine: He has not got the super licence points yet.

payload.prompt: Which team has won the most constructors' titles?

options.text: Ferrari, with 16.
options.explanation: Right. Ferrari holds the record, with Williams next on 9.

options.text: Mercedes, with 16.
options.explanation: Mercedes has won eight, all in a row from 2014 to 2021.

options.text: Red Bull, with 16.
options.explanation: Red Bull has won several, but not sixteen.

options.text: McLaren, with 16.
options.explanation: McLaren has won fewer than Ferrari.

explanation.correct: Ferrari has won 16 constructors' titles, more than any other team.
explanation.incorrect: Ferrari is the record holder with 16. Others, such as Williams, McLaren and Mercedes, are well behind.
explanation.sayThisLine: Ferrari has the record for team titles.

payload.prompt: Complete the Triple Crown.
payload.template: The Triple Crown is the Monaco Grand Prix, the Indianapolis 500 and the 24 Hours of {{race}}.

explanation.correct: The Triple Crown of Motorsport is Monaco, the Indy 500 and Le Mans. Graham Hill is the only driver to have won all three.
explanation.incorrect: The third leg is the 24 Hours of Le Mans.
explanation.sayThisLine: Only Graham Hill has won the Triple Crown.

lessons.title: Talk and season refresh
lessons.objective: Retrieve how to chat about the season without faking it.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: Hamilton is the greatest of all time, end of discussion.

payload.question: What keeps it a fun chat?

options.text: Say what you like about him and ask who else she rates, since there is no single right answer.
options.explanation: Right. The greatest-ever debate is a taste argument, not a fact.

options.text: Tell her she is wrong and list your own favourite's stats.
options.explanation: Facts do not settle taste, and it will end the fun.

options.text: Agree with everything so there is no argument.
options.explanation: Empty agreement is dull. Bring a genuine opinion or question.

options.text: Claim you watched every one of his races.
options.explanation: Do not fake expertise. Honest curiosity is better.

payload.translation: Who is the greatest is a taste argument. Share something you genuinely like and ask who else she rates.

followUps.line: Which of his seasons do you rate most?
followUps.why: It lets her tell a story rather than a verdict.

followUps.line: Who is the best you have seen?
followUps.why: It keeps the conversation going.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You do not need stats. Ask her what she has loved watching.

payload.prompt: She says the stewards robbed her driver. Best first reply?

scene.alt: Text only: a fan is upset about a stewards' decision.

explanation.correct: Asking what she saw lets her explain and feel heard. You can look at the stewards' reasons together later.
explanation.incorrect: Quoting rules, especially ones you may not know, tends to start an argument. Asking is warmer.
explanation.sayThisLine: Tell me what you saw, and what made it unfair.

payload.prompt: A fast team keeps retiring. What is the problem called?

options.text: Reliability
options.explanation: Right. Reliability is about the car finishing races.

options.text: Downforce
options.explanation: Downforce is about grip, not finishing.

options.text: Parc ferme
options.explanation: That is about locking the set-up after qualifying.

options.text: Track limits
options.explanation: Track limits are about staying within the white lines.

explanation.correct: Reliability is how often the car finishes. A fast car that keeps retiring scores no points, as a DNF is worth zero.
explanation.incorrect: Retiring repeatedly is a reliability problem. Speed does not help if the car does not finish.
explanation.sayThisLine: They have the pace but not the reliability.

payload.prompt: Complete the rumour rule.
payload.template: Until a team {{does}} it, a driver move is only a {{what}}.

explanation.correct: A move is official only when the team or driver announces it. Until then, it is silly season talk.
explanation.incorrect: Until a team announces a move, it is a rumour, however many people repeat it.
explanation.sayThisLine: It is a rumour until the team confirms it.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: Nothing went right today. Strategy, pace, everything.

payload.question: What is the warmest reply?

options.text: That sounds rough. What was the one thing you were hoping to see?
options.explanation: Right. You acknowledge the feeling and invite her to share.

options.text: Well, at least the season is long.
options.explanation: It may be true, but it skips her feelings.

options.text: Maybe you should pick a winning team.
options.explanation: Fandom is not about winning, and it is unkind.

options.text: I could have told you that would happen.
options.explanation: Nobody likes an I-told-you-so, and you would be faking it.

payload.translation: When someone has had a bad day, listen first and ask what they were hoping for.

followUps.line: Was it the car or the strategy?
followUps.why: A follow-up that helps her think it through once she is ready.

followUps.line: What would fix it for next time?
followUps.why: It turns disappointment into hope.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You do not need to fix it. Listening and a gentle question are enough.
